questions.q: What does CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) do?
options: Builds a brand-new table directly from a query's result set, with column names and types inferred from the query
Only inserts rows into a table that must already exist with a matching schema
Deletes a table and all of its data permanently
Grants permissions on an existing table
questions.explain: CTAS creates the table and populates it from the SELECT's result set in one statement, with no separate CREATE TABLE and column list needed.

questions.q: What happens if you run a plain CREATE TABLE AS SELECT a second time against the same table name?
options: It errors out because the table already exists
It silently appends the new rows to the existing table
It automatically renames the old table and creates a new one
It merges the new result set into the existing rows
questions.explain: Plain CTAS fails on a rerun since the table name is already taken — this is exactly why CREATE OR REPLACE is used for rerunnable pipelines.

questions.q: Why is CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT the form typically used in a scheduled ELT pipeline?
options: It atomically swaps the old table for the fresh result set in one operation, so it's safe to rerun unattended
It runs faster than every other type of SQL statement in Snowflake
It is the only syntax Snowflake allows for creating tables
It automatically emails an alert when the table changes
questions.explain: CREATE OR REPLACE avoids the 'table already exists' failure of plain CTAS by atomically replacing the table, making it the idiom for pipelines that rerun on a schedule.

questions.q: How does Snowflake's CTAS pattern compare to T-SQL's SELECT ... INTO?
options: The core idea is the same, but in Snowflake, drop-and-rebuild via CREATE OR REPLACE is the default idiom rather than a workaround bolted on afterward
SELECT INTO and CTAS have no similarities at all
CTAS cannot infer column types the way SELECT INTO does
SELECT INTO is safe to rerun without any changes, unlike CTAS
questions.explain: Both build a table from a query, but Snowflake treats CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE AS SELECT as the standard rerunnable pattern, whereas SELECT INTO in T-SQL errors on a second run just like plain CTAS does.

questions.q: Where does business logic like casts, CASE expressions, and filters belong when transforming data with CTAS?
options: Directly inside the SELECT statement that feeds the CTAS — there's no separate transformation layer to configure
In a separate ETL tool that runs before the data reaches Snowflake
In a stored procedure that must run before every CTAS statement
Business logic cannot be applied during a CTAS statement
questions.explain: Since CTAS materializes whatever the SELECT produces, all business logic — casts, calculated columns, CASE expressions, filters — is written directly into that SELECT.
